question: In a child with an acute variceal haemorrhage, IV terlipressin or octreotide should be started immediately as a pharmacological measure to reduce portal pressure, alongside fluid resuscitation, before endoscopic therapy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is TRUE. Pharmacological therapy (terlipressin or octreotide/somatostatin) BEFORE endoscopy is standard practice for variceal bleeding. These agents reduce splanchnic blood flow, lowering portal pressure and slowing bleeding. They are started immediately and continued for 2–5 days. Endoscopy (EVL or sclerotherapy) follows within 12–24 hours to achieve definitive haemostasis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The acute management of variceal haemorrhage follows a rapid sequence: (1) ABC resuscitation — IV access, blood transfusion (target Hb 7–8 g/dL; over-transfusion worsens portal pressure), (2) pharmacological vasoconstriction — terlipressin (vasopressin analogue) or octreotide (somatostatin analogue) IV to reduce splanchnic blood flow, (3) antibiotics (ceftriaxone to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), (4) urgent endoscopy within 12–24 hours for variceal ligation or sclerotherapy. Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube) is a last resort only.
